item.title: The Digital Iron Curtain
item.description: Having strangled the traditional press, the Russian state now moves to sever its own people from the open internet — throttling and listing the platforms that carry voices at odds with Kremlin propaganda, while protecting the messenger aligned with it. And in doing so it collides with a fact larger than itself: the global platforms have become powers in their own right, rivals of states for the human mind.

item.title: Confronting Personified Evil: The Logic of Eliminating a Dictator
item.description: There are rare moments when global evil concentrates in a single human body. Eliminating such a figure can be a legitimate way to end a war — but the deciding factor is political will, and the only thing that manufactures that will, or forbids it, is the deterrent the man stands behind.

item.title: The Suppression Machine: How Dictatorships Manufacture Obedience
item.description: A dictator commands no superpowers, yet millions obey. The answer lies not in the people's character but in a machine of suppression, negative selection, and institutionalized distrust that isolates every individual against the whole.

item.title: Who Actually Supports This War: The Politics of Passive Complicity
item.description: An attempt to count, honestly, who stands behind the war against Ukraine — and to show why the silent majority's head-in-the-sand stance amounts, politically, to support, even as it differs morally from the howling of the propagandists.

item.title: An Idea Is Not an Ideology: Why the 'Russian World' Cannot Reshape History
item.description: Putin and Trump cannot bend history the way Lenin or Genghis Khan did, because they have only power and money where those figures had a guiding idea. The "Russian world" is an idea, but never an ideology — it points only backward, which is why no one else has ever adopted it.

item.title: Russia Has Never Had a Free Press: Propaganda Is Not Journalism
item.description: Russia's press was never an information service; it was born as an instrument of propaganda. And propaganda, being a chemical blow to public consciousness, is not journalism at all but something closer to a controlled substance.

item.title: Chaos as a Product: How Trump Governs and Who Benefits
item.description: Trump's presidency does not produce a strategy; it produces chaos. This essay argues that the swings, the broken promises, and the endless "two more weeks" are not a hidden plan but the product itself, and that in the short term the confusion serves the man who manufactures death.

item.title: Shura Burtin’s Journalism on Russia’s War in Ukraine: Themes, Tone, and Bias
item.description: A comprehensive review of Shura Burtin’s body of journalistic work, focusing on recurring themes, political framing, and his portrayals of Ukraine and Russia.

item.title: Postmodern Fascism: Trumpism as a New Form of the Old Disease
item.description: Trumpism is not ordinary right-wing populism but a postmodern mutation of fascism, built on lying without precedent and the open contempt for empathy — and it is uniquely dangerous because it has captured a still-free democracy.

item.title: Words Are Deeds: Against the Counsel to Ignore What Leaders Say
item.description: A defense of taking political rhetoric seriously: the words of the powerful are themselves a material force that moves markets, launders aggression, and reshapes what people plan and do. The fashionable advice to judge leaders only by deeds is not worldly wisdom but a disarming mistake.

item.title: Weaponizing History
item.description: A regime that can promise no future seizes the past instead. The Russian state has declared a monopoly on history — rewriting textbooks to manufacture obedient generations, criminalising dissenting memory by law, demolishing the institutions that hold the record of its own crimes, and replacing real history with a victory cult and a lost-paradise myth. But history is a science, not retrospective politics, and the weaponising of the past is a boomerang.

item.title: The Orthodox Church as the Engine of the War
item.description: The comfortable view holds that the Russian Orthodox Church is a faith the regime merely co-opts. The truth is harder: the Moscow Patriarchate in its present form is a security-service fabrication, rebuilt by Stalin's NKVD and vetted by the organs ever since — and it now supplies the invasion with its sacred justification, recasting aggression as holy war, telling soldiers that killing washes away sin, and building a state cult of death. But the engine is failing with the empire it serves.
